claims.text: 3D ink-extrusion printing of powder-loaded inks can reduce the sintering temperature required for densification.
The proposed starting materials are powdered refractory alloys or high-entropy alloys prepared for additive manufacturing.
The intervention deposits a powder-loaded ink at room temperature to form a green part.
Layered ink deposition can be followed by sintering at a lower temperature than conventional powder metallurgy.
Ink-extrusion printing produces a homogeneous distribution of fine powders in the green part.
The printed green part has shorter particle-contact distances than conventionally prepared powder compacts.
Ink-extrusion printing produces more uniform particle packing.
Room-temperature ink deposition improves microstructural control and reduces defects.
Shorter diffusion distances and fewer defects facilitate sintering and densification.
Facilitated diffusion and densification permit sintering at lower temperatures than are required for conventional pre-compacted powders.
Lower-temperature sintering of ink-extruded parts can achieve densification comparable to traditional high-temperature sintering.
Lower-temperature sintering of ink-extruded parts can achieve mechanical properties comparable to traditional high-temperature sintering.
Laser melting deposition and laser powder bed fusion have been used to additively manufacture refractory high-entropy alloys.
Conventional powder metallurgy, laser melting deposition, or laser powder bed fusion requires higher sintering temperatures than ink-extrusion printing.
Laser-based additive manufacturing incurs thermal stresses during processing.
The proposed approach is limited to powders that can be loaded suitably into printable inks.
The sintering-temperature reduction may depend on the alloy system and powder formulation.
The magnitude of the temperature reduction and its effects on microstructure and performance remain to be quantitatively validated across alloy systems.
